screens.title: Virtual Machine Creation and Lifecycle with virsh
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn a practical, command-line-first workflow for creating and managing KVM virtual machines. We focus on virt-install for repeatable provisioning and virsh for inspecting, editing, and controlling VM state. You will see how a single virt-install command builds a machine image, defines its hardware, and starts installation, and how the VM XML is the authoritative configuration that libvirt uses. We cover safe editing practices, which changes can be applied live, and when to shut down a guest. You will also practice hot-plugging disks and network interfaces with --live and --persistent options so changes are both immediate and durable. Finally, we emphasize naming and image-management practices that reduce orphaned storage and simplify automation. By the end of this lesson you will be able to script VM creation, validate and edit XML definitions, and manage VMs reliably on headless hosts. Think of this chapter as the CLI toolkit you need to provision clusters and run production VMs without a graphical console. What repeatable step will you automate first?

screens.title: virt-install: a reproducible provisioning command
screens.narratorSegment: Virt-install is the workhorse for scripted VM provisioning. It accepts options that fully describe the virtual hardware and installation method so you can run identical commands in automation. When you run virt-install with name, R A M, vcpus, disk, network, and cdrom or location flags, libvirt creates a disk image, defines the VM XML, and starts the guest to begin OS installation. For example, creating a RHEL 9 test VM with 4GB of R A M, two vCPUs, a 30GB qcow2 disk, bridged networking to br0, and booting from a local ISO is a single command. Notice options like --noautoconsole so the command does not try to attach a console, and --graphics to control VNC or headless modes. This pattern matters because it lets you template a command for many servers, or drive it from automation tools. A common misconception is that virt-install only handles the initial install; in truth it produces a persistent libvirt definition you can later edit with virsh. Practice by preparing an images directory and running a single virt-install command, then confirm the new machine appears in virsh list --all.

keyIdea.title: One command, repeatable VMs
keyIdea.text: Use virt-install parameters to fully specify and script VM creation so deployments are consistent.

content.html:
Core Concept
virt-install anatomy
A single virt-install command can define hardware, storage, network, and start installation immediately—ideal for automation.
Example command
sudo virt-install \
  --name rhel9-webserver \
  --ram 4096 \
  --vcpus 2 \
  --disk path=/var/lib/libvirt/images/rhel9-webserver.qcow2,size=30,format=qcow2 \
  --network bridge=br0 \
  --os-variant rhel9.0 \
  --cdrom /var/lib/libvirt/images/rhel-9.0-x86_64-dvd.iso \
  --graphics vnc,listen=0.0.0.0 \
  --noautoconsole \
  --boot cdrom,hd,network
What each option means
  • --name: unique VM identifier used by libvirt and virsh.
  • --ram / --vcpus: resource allocation that should reflect host capacity.
  • --disk: creates or points to a qcow2 image; size and format are explicit.
  • --network: connect to a bridge like br0 for external access.
  • --cdrom / --location: installation source; use network sources for automation.
Example
Run the command, connect with a VNC client, complete installation, then shut down and verify the VM is defined in libvirt.
Key Takeaway
Virt-install provides a single, scriptable entry point to define VM hardware and start installs, enabling automation and consistency.

screens.title: Detailed virt-install parameters and practical choices
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing virt-install parameters affects automation and post-install configuration. You must decide whether to use a CD-ROM ISO, a network installation source, or a location URL. For automated runs, a network source plus --initrd-inject and --extra-args with a kickstart file removes manual steps. Network options matter: bridging to br0 exposes the guest to the host network, while NAT or macvtap have different isolation properties. Graphics choices define console access; --graphics none is common for fully automated, headless installs, while VNC or spice are used when you need an interactive installer. Use --noautoconsole to prevent the command from blocking your terminal, and consider --wait to control how long virt-install waits for the VM to shut down. Common misconceptions include thinking that changing the command after installation will retroactively change an existing VM; in fact, virt-install sets the initial XML and images — further changes require virsh or editing the XML. As a rule, prepare your image directory, ensure ISO or network paths are reachable, and script the full command in your automation tool. Detailed virt-install parameters and practical choices means select installation source, network mode, and console options to match your automation and access requirements.. In practical terms, choose the right flags for automation, networking, and console access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition
Parameter selection
Match flags to your deployment model: interactive vs automated, bridged vs isolated networking, and persistent disk expectations.
Automation tips
Prefer network installs and kickstart for unattended deployments; use --graphics none and --noautoconsole when no interactive console is needed.
Networking considerations
Bridging to br0 provides direct network access; ensure firewall and bridge configuration is correct before provisioning.
Parameter quick-reference
--cdrom
Local ISO for interactive installs
--location / --pxe
Use for network installs and automation
--noautoconsole
Prevent console attachment from blocking scripts
--graphics none
Headless installs suitable for automation
Misconception
Changing the virt-install command does not alter an already-created VM; use virsh and edit the XML for post-creation changes.

screens.title: VM XML definition: the authoritative configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Every VM defined by libvirt has an XML document that records its hardware, resources, boot order, and attached devices. This XML is the canonical source for libvirt and is what virsh uses when starting or redefining a guest. You can view it with virsh dumpxml. Editing is done with virsh edit, which opens the XML in your default editor and validates syntax on save. Key sections include for boot devices, and for resources, and for disks and network interfaces. A frequent change is reordering the elements so that the hard disk boots before a CD-ROM. Be careful: some edits require the VM to be shut down to take effect, while others can be hot-plugged. A common mistake is modifying XML without preserving device addresses or targets, which can change device enumeration inside the guest. Always validate the XML, and consider exporting a copy before large changes. Practically, after you edit, test by starting the VM and confirming the expected behavior in the guest OS. VM XML definition: the authoritative configuration means use virsh dumpxml and virsh edit to inspect and persist configuration; validate syntax and understand which edits require shutdown.. In practical terms, understanding dumpxml, the structure, and safe edits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: XML is authoritative
keyIdea.text: Use virsh dumpxml and virsh edit to inspect and persist configuration; validate syntax and understand which edits require shutdown.

content.html:
Definition
VM XML structure
The XML contains the VM's <os>, <devices>, and resource elements that libvirt reads at runtime.
Example — change boot order
<os>
  <type arch='x86_64' machine='pc-q35-6.2'>hvm</type>
  <boot dev='hd' />
  <boot dev='network' />
</os>
How to edit safely
  • Use virsh edit <VM> so libvirt validates on save.
  • Export a backup copy with virsh dumpxml > vmname.xml before large edits.
  • Mind device targets and addresses to avoid renaming or reordering disks inside the guest.
Common mistake
Editing XML while a VM is running and expecting all changes to apply immediately; some must be applied with virsh set* commands or after reboot.
Key Takeaway
Treat the XML as the single source of truth and validate edits before restarting or applying them to running guests.

screens.title: Live changes vs persistent configuration
screens.narratorSegment: When managing configuration changes, you must decide if they should apply immediately to a running VM, be saved for the next boot, or both. The --live flag attempts to apply a change to the running guest, while --persistent writes the change into the VM's XML so it survives restarts. For example, attaching a disk with virsh attach-disk and using --live --persistent both hot-plugs the device and records it in the XML. Some operations cannot be applied live: changing C P U architecture or removing the primary disk typically requires shutting down the guest. A frequent pitfall is editing XML without applying live changes and assuming the guest will reflect them immediately. Conversely, applying --live without --persistent means the change is lost on reboot. Use comparison cards to decide: need immediate access and a durable config — use both flags; need temporary test — use --live only; changing an incompatible attribute — shut down and edit XML. Always confirm in the guest OS that new devices are present after a live attach and monitor logs for errors. Live changes vs persistent configuration means use --live to apply immediately and --persistent to save changes. use both when you need immediate and durable changes.. In practical terms, when to use --live and --persistent, and what to expect. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Choose live vs persistent
keyIdea.text: Use --live to apply immediately and --persistent to save changes. Use both when you need immediate and durable changes.

content.html:
Process Flow
Live vs Persistent changes
Decide if a change should be immediate, durable, or both before running virsh commands.
--live
Attempts to apply change to running VM; may fail for incompatible changes.
--persistent
Saves the change into the VM XML so it persists across reboots.
Decision matrix
Immediate and durable
Use --live --persistent when hot-plugging disks or NICs into production services that must remain available.
Temporary test
Use --live only for experiments that should be removed on reboot.
Requires shutdown
Changes like CPU architecture updates require shutdown and XML edits without --live applicability.
Key Takeaway
Plan whether a change must be immediate and persistent before running virsh to avoid unintended transient state or lost edits.

screens.title: Essential virsh lifecycle commands
screens.narratorSegment: Virsh is the primary tool for VM lifecycle management. Start by listing VMs with virsh list --all to see running and shut-off guests. Use virsh start to power on a defined VM, and virsh shutdown to request an ACPI-based graceful shutdown from the guest OS. If the guest is unresponsive or you need an immediate stop, virsh destroy performs a forceful power off — similar to pulling the power cord — and can cause filesystem corruption if used indiscriminately. Rebooting uses virsh reboot. To pause execution without freeing memory, virsh suspend suspends to R A M and virsh resume resumes it. When you want to remove a VM from libvirt, virsh undefine deletes the definition but leaves disk images intact, so be sure to remove or migrate images as needed. Autostart controls whether a VM starts with the host using virsh autostart and virsh autostart --disable. Practice: define a VM, start it, request a graceful shutdown, and only use destroy when graceful shutdown fails. This pattern reduces data-loss risk and keeps hosts stable. Essential virsh lifecycle commands means use virsh list, start, shutdown, destroy, reboot, suspend, resume, undefine, and autostart to manage vm states safely.. In practical terms, commands to list, start, shutdown, force stop, reboot, suspend, resume, and undefine vms. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle control with virsh
keyIdea.text: Use virsh list, start, shutdown, destroy, reboot, suspend, resume, undefine, and autostart to manage VM states safely.

content.html:
Process Flow
Core virsh commands
Control VM state and startup behavior using a small set of well-understood commands.
virsh list --all
virsh start <VM_NAME>
virsh shutdown <VM_NAME>
virsh destroy <VM_NAME>
virsh reboot <VM_NAME>
virsh suspend <VM_NAME>
virsh resume <VM_NAME>
virsh undefine <VM_NAME>
virsh autostart <VM_NAME>  # enable
virsh autostart --disable <VM_NAME>  # disable
Interpretation
  • Prefer graceful shutdown to avoid data corruption.
  • Use destroy only as a last resort; check guest logs afterwards.
  • Undefine removes the libvirt record but not disk images.
Common mistake
Using destroy regularly in production can lead to filesystem corruption; always attempt shutdown first.
Key Takeaway
Learn the difference between graceful and forceful operations and protect guest data by using the correct virsh command for the situation.

screens.title: Attaching and detaching disks and network interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: Hot-plugging devices is a powerful capability for managing live systems. Using virsh attach-disk you can add a qcow2 image to a running VM, and with --live the change is attempted immediately. Adding --persistent writes the disk into the VM XML so it remains after reboot. For example, attach a data disk with virsh attach-disk --domain rhel9-webserver --source /var/lib/libvirt/images/data_disk. qcow2 --target vdb --persistent --live. After attaching, verify inside the guest that the device appears and is partitioned and mounted as required. To remove a disk, use virsh detach-disk; be sure to unmount and flush writes in the guest first. For NICs, virsh attach-interface and detach-interface perform similar operations. Misconceptions include assuming hot-plug always succeeds: the guest OS and device model must support the change, and you may need drivers or rescan actions. Always test hot-plug workflows in a staging environment and ensure backups are taken before reconfiguring production disks. Attaching and detaching disks and network interfaces means attach or detach disks and nics with virsh using --live for immediate effect and --persistent to save configuration.. In practical terms, hot-plug storage and nics with --live and record with --persistent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Troubles happen, and understanding common mistakes shortens troubleshooting time. One major issue is using virsh destroy without attempting shutdown first; this risks filesystem corruption. If destroy was used, check guest logs and run filesystem checks after booting to assess damage. Another frequent problem is orphaned disk images: administrators undefine VMs but forget to remove or migrate the image files. Maintain a cleanup checklist that first verifies images are not referenced by any VM and then archives or deletes them. Hot-plug failures often stem from guest OS limitations or missing drivers; review dmesg and kernel logs and perform a rescan in the guest or add drivers. XML syntax errors caused by manual edits are caught by libvirt validation, but keep backups of dumpxml output to restore known-good state. For performance issues, examine host-level overcommit and reduce allocations or migrate VMs. A practical troubleshooting habit is to reproduce the change in a staging VM, confirm result, then apply it to production during a maintenance window. Comparison
Mistake vs Safe Alternative
Using destroy indiscriminately
Risk: data corruption. Safe alternative: attempt virsh shutdown, check guest status, then use destroy only if necessary after graceful attempts fail.
Undefining without image cleanup
Risk: orphan images consuming storage. Safe alternative: list image files, archive or move before deleting definitions, and use a documented cleanup process.
Hot-plug failures
Risk: device not recognized. Safe alternative: verify guest support, check dmesg, and test in staging before production hot-plug.
Troubleshooting checklist
  1. Confirm VM state with virsh list --all.

  3. Restore XML from backup if edits fail validation.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn a practical, command-line-first workflow for creating and managing KVM virtual machines. We focus on virt-install for repeatable provisioning and virsh for inspecting, editing, and controlling VM state. You will see how a single virt-install command builds a machine image, defines its hardware, and starts installation, and how the VM XML is the authoritative configuration that libvirt uses. We cover safe editing practices, which changes can be applied live, and when to shut down a guest. You will also practice hot-plugging disks and network interfaces with --live and --persistent options so changes are both immediate and durable. Finally, we emphasize naming and image-management practices that reduce orphaned storage and simplify automation. By the end of this lesson you will be able to script VM creation, validate and edit XML definitions, and manage VMs reliably on headless hosts. Think of this chapter as the CLI toolkit you need to provision clusters and run production VMs without a graphical console. What repeatable step will you automate first?

These objectives guide practical skills you will use daily as an architect. First, you will create KVM virtual machines from scratch using virt-install, learning to supply name, resources, disks, network, and installation source in a single scripted command so deployments are repeatable. Second, you will view and edit a VM's XML definition, understanding the XML schema as libvirt's authoritative configuration and how to change boot order, devices, and resources safely. Third, you will use virsh to manage VM lifecycle operations such as start, shutdown, destroy, suspend, resume, and undefine, and understand the risks of forceful actions. Finally on this screen you will learn to attach and detach disks and network interfaces both live and persistently, using --live and --persistent flags to apply immediate changes while keeping the configuration durable. Each skill includes a competence milestone so you can verify you performed the action correctly on a host. These objectives focus on automation, safety, and repeatability for production-grade VM management.

This second objectives screen expands into operational skills you need when managing many VMs. You will learn naming and image-management best practices to avoid orphaned storage and make automation simpler: consistent name schemes and organized image directories reduce mistakes in the long run. You will understand resource allocation trade-offs so you avoid over-provisioning the host or starving guests; monitoring metrics guide resizing. You will practice autostart configuration to ensure critical VMs restart with the host, and how to disable autostart for maintenance windows. Finally, you will learn to use templates and unattended installation techniques, such as injecting kickstart or using a network installation source, to scale deployments of identical VMs. Each card includes a brief mnemonic and a milestone so you can confirm the host follows these best practices in your lab or production environment.

Virt-install is the workhorse for scripted VM provisioning. It accepts options that fully describe the virtual hardware and installation method so you can run identical commands in automation. When you run virt-install with name, R A M, vcpus, disk, network, and cdrom or location flags, libvirt creates a disk image, defines the VM XML, and starts the guest to begin OS installation. For example, creating a RHEL 9 test VM with 4GB of R A M, two vCPUs, a 30GB qcow2 disk, bridged networking to br0, and booting from a local ISO is a single command. Notice options like --noautoconsole so the command does not try to attach a console, and --graphics to control VNC or headless modes. This pattern matters because it lets you template a command for many servers, or drive it from automation tools. A common misconception is that virt-install only handles the initial install; in truth it produces a persistent libvirt definition you can later edit with virsh. Practice by preparing an images directory and running a single virt-install command, then confirm the new machine appears in virsh list --all.

Choosing virt-install parameters affects automation and post-install configuration. You must decide whether to use a CD-ROM ISO, a network installation source, or a location URL. For automated runs, a network source plus --initrd-inject and --extra-args with a kickstart file removes manual steps. Network options matter: bridging to br0 exposes the guest to the host network, while NAT or macvtap have different isolation properties. Graphics choices define console access; --graphics none is common for fully automated, headless installs, while VNC or spice are used when you need an interactive installer. Use --noautoconsole to prevent the command from blocking your terminal, and consider --wait to control how long virt-install waits for the VM to shut down. Common misconceptions include thinking that changing the command after installation will retroactively change an existing VM; in fact, virt-install sets the initial XML and images — further changes require virsh or editing the XML. As a rule, prepare your image directory, ensure ISO or network paths are reachable, and script the full command in your automation tool. Detailed virt-install parameters and practical choices means select installation source, network mode, and console options to match your automation and access requirements.. In practical terms, choose the right flags for automation, networking, and console access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Every VM defined by libvirt has an XML document that records its hardware, resources, boot order, and attached devices. This XML is the canonical source for libvirt and is what virsh uses when starting or redefining a guest. You can view it with virsh dumpxml. Editing is done with virsh edit, which opens the XML in your default editor and validates syntax on save. Key sections include for boot devices, and for resources, and for disks and network interfaces. A frequent change is reordering the elements so that the hard disk boots before a CD-ROM. Be careful: some edits require the VM to be shut down to take effect, while others can be hot-plugged. A common mistake is modifying XML without preserving device addresses or targets, which can change device enumeration inside the guest. Always validate the XML, and consider exporting a copy before large changes. Practically, after you edit, test by starting the VM and confirming the expected behavior in the guest OS. VM XML definition: the authoritative configuration means use virsh dumpxml and virsh edit to inspect and persist configuration; validate syntax and understand which edits require shutdown.. In practical terms, understanding dumpxml, the structure, and safe edits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When managing configuration changes, you must decide if they should apply immediately to a running VM, be saved for the next boot, or both. The --live flag attempts to apply a change to the running guest, while --persistent writes the change into the VM's XML so it survives restarts. For example, attaching a disk with virsh attach-disk and using --live --persistent both hot-plugs the device and records it in the XML. Some operations cannot be applied live: changing C P U architecture or removing the primary disk typically requires shutting down the guest. A frequent pitfall is editing XML without applying live changes and assuming the guest will reflect them immediately. Conversely, applying --live without --persistent means the change is lost on reboot. Use comparison cards to decide: need immediate access and a durable config — use both flags; need temporary test — use --live only; changing an incompatible attribute — shut down and edit XML. Always confirm in the guest OS that new devices are present after a live attach and monitor logs for errors. Live changes vs persistent configuration means use --live to apply immediately and --persistent to save changes. use both when you need immediate and durable changes.. In practical terms, when to use --live and --persistent, and what to expect. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Virsh is the primary tool for VM lifecycle management. Start by listing VMs with virsh list --all to see running and shut-off guests. Use virsh start to power on a defined VM, and virsh shutdown to request an ACPI-based graceful shutdown from the guest OS. If the guest is unresponsive or you need an immediate stop, virsh destroy performs a forceful power off — similar to pulling the power cord — and can cause filesystem corruption if used indiscriminately. Rebooting uses virsh reboot. To pause execution without freeing memory, virsh suspend suspends to R A M and virsh resume resumes it. When you want to remove a VM from libvirt, virsh undefine deletes the definition but leaves disk images intact, so be sure to remove or migrate images as needed. Autostart controls whether a VM starts with the host using virsh autostart and virsh autostart --disable. Practice: define a VM, start it, request a graceful shutdown, and only use destroy when graceful shutdown fails. This pattern reduces data-loss risk and keeps hosts stable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception.
